title: Rome has not defined that faith is unnecessary for a morally good act: Jansenius
source_text: LI. Apparet quoque ex iis quae supra retulimus, contrariam sententiam, quae statuit fidem in Christum necessariam non esse, ad hoc ut aliquis bene moraliter operetur, in Ecclesia Romana non ita certam & definitam esse, ut contrarium tenere non liceat; quandoquidem Jansenius, & qui eum sequuntur insignes viri non pauci, idem hac in parte cum Protestantibus aperte docent, nec propterea tamen, ut propter alia multa, publica censura fuit notatus Jansenii liber.
pass_a_gloss: LI. It appears also from those things which we related above, that the contrary opinion, which lays down that faith in Christ is not necessary, for this that someone work morally well, in the Roman Church is not so certain and defined, that it is not lawful to hold the contrary; since Jansenius, and not a few distinguished men who follow him, openly teach the same in this part with the Protestants, nor on that account however, as on account of many other things, was the book of Jansenius marked with public censure.
pass_b_english: Thesis LI. It also appears from what we reported above that the opposite view, which holds that faith in Christ is not necessary for someone to act morally well, is not so certain and defined in the Roman Church that it is forbidden to hold the contrary.

For Jansenius, and a good number of distinguished men who follow him, openly teach the same as the Protestants on this point, and yet Jansenius's book was not publicly censured for this, as it was for many other things.

choices.why: Official condemnation; the Augustinus was condemned by Urban VIII (In eminenti, dated 1642, published 1643) and its five propositions by Innocent X (Cum occasione, 1653), but not for this point.
